title: The Robot I Saw at a Spelling Bee
excerpt: I went to a spelling bee. I came back with an obsession. In 2018, an old friend showed me a robot he'd built — and nothing about my plans looked the same after that.
content:
#
**2018 — JHS**

I didn't go to DPS looking for robots. I went for a spelling bee.

That's the part I always have to remind myself of when I tell this story — none of it was planned. It was just a normal inter-school competition, the kind where you show up, do your thing, and go home. Except that day, going home wasn't the end of it.

While I was there, I ran into an old friend — Chris, someone who used to be at my school before he moved to DPS. We hadn't seen each other in a while, so naturally we got talking, catching up on everything that had changed. And then, almost as a side note, he showed me something he'd been building.

I don't think I can fully describe what that moment did to me. I was looking at an actual robot — something a student, someone my age, had built with his own hands. Not something from a textbook or a video. Something real, sitting right there.

I was smitten. Genuinely. There's no better word for it.

What made it hit even harder was the contrast. My own school didn't have anything like this. No robotics setup, no lab full of wires and motors, nothing. So this wasn't just "oh that's cool" — it was the first time I understood that this was even a thing I could do. That kids were doing it. That it wasn't locked away in some world I didn't have access to.

I didn't build anything that day. I didn't even touch the robot, if I remember right. But something shifted. A door opened that I didn't know existed, and even though I wouldn't walk through it properly for a few more years, I never really forgot it was there.

Looking back now, this is where it all starts — not with a class, not with a teacher pushing me toward it, but with a spelling bee I almost didn't think twice about, and Chris, a friend who happened to be building something incredible on the side.

*Next: SHS1, and the mentor who helped shape everything that came after.*

*— A3PK Labs*

title: Rebuilding Albert.dev: From Portfolio Template to Engineering Workshop
excerpt: A build log on why I tore down my portfolio and rebuilt it as a lab, not a resume.
content:
A build log on why I tore down my portfolio and rebuilt it as a lab, not a resume.

---

## The Problem With "Before"

For a while, my portfolio did what most student portfolios do: it introduced me, listed some skills as percentage bars, and showed a grid of project cards. It worked. It just didn't sound like me.

Here's what it looked like.

### Hero

![Before — Hero section](/images/before-hero.png)

Clean, readable, standard. "Tech Enthusiast & Developer" is accurate but generic — it could describe thousands of student portfolios. There's no voice here, no hint of how I actually think or build.

### About

![Before — About section 1](/images/before-about-1.png)
![Before — About section 2](/images/before-about-2.png)

The bio is honest — lifelong learner, Python + web platforms, Tema, Ghana, 20 years old. But it reads like a LinkedIn summary rather than something written by someone who documents failed prototypes for fun.

### Skills

![Before — Skills section](/images/before-skills.png)

Percentage bars are a common pattern, but they invite an obvious question: what does "Python — 85%" actually mean? There's no receipts behind the number — no link to the thing I built that proves it.

### Projects

![Before — Projects section](/images/before-projects.png)

This is the section that bothered me most. Several cards — Bible Stories, GospelHelper, AIResearch, Thoughtholder — shared the exact same placeholder line: *"A software project developed to solve real-world tasks. Click GitHub to see more details."* Only one project (LifeOS) had a real description. To a visitor, that reads as unfinished, not curated.

---

## The Rebuild: Thinking Like a Workshop, Not a Resume

The fix wasn't just a new color palette. It was a change in framing. Instead of presenting myself as a finished product ("Tech Enthusiast & Developer"), I wanted the site to read like an active lab — a place documenting real builds, real iterations, and real failures, in progress.

That's where the terminal/dev-console identity came from: **Build. Break. Learn. Repeat.** — the same line I use for A3PK Labs. The site had to sound like the person actually behind it.

### Hero

![After — Hero section](/images/after-hero.png)

The `STATUS: EXPLORING NEW IDEAS` badge replaces the static tagline with something that feels alive. The typed command-line intro ties directly into my content voice instead of sitting apart from it. The mascot on the right reinforces "workshop" over "resume."

### About

![After — About section](/images/after-about.png)

`IDENTITY_QUERY.sh` and `ACTIVE_EXPLORATIONS.md` turn the About section into something that feels native to how I actually work — files, logs, active experiments — rather than a bio paragraph competing with empty whitespace.

### Projects

![After — Workshop/Projects section](/images/after-workshop.png)

Reframed as a **Repository Index**. Each project is a Build Log with a version tag, status (`IN PROGRESS` / `STABLE`), a real one-line mission statement, and a tech stack — no more placeholder copy.

### The Console

![After — Terminal easter egg](/images/after-terminal.png)

This is the piece I'm most excited about. A functional `DEV_CONSOLE.bin` with real commands — `about`, `skills`, `projects`, `journal`, `resume`, even a `sudo` login gate — turns the portfolio itself into a small interactive artifact.

---

## Why This Matters

The percentage bars and placeholder cards weren't *wrong*, exactly — they were just impersonal. Anyone could have that portfolio. The rebuild isn't really about dark mode versus light mode. It's about making the site sound like it was built by someone who documents failure states and half-finished prototypes on purpose, because that's the actual process — not just the polished outcome.

title: IEEE x GDG x Aaenics Hackathon Highlights & Pitching Takeaways
excerpt: Attended a combined IEEE, GDG, and Aaenics hackathon at Longjii Hotel. Observations on a winning idea, key takeaways on problem-first pitch strategies, and personal event reflections.
content:
## Overview
Attended a combined hackathon hosted by IEEE, GDG, and Aaenics at Longjii Hotel. The event brought together student developers, organizers, and judges for a fast-paced solution-building session.

---

## Event Timeline & Experience
* **Preparation & Arrival:** Prepped early in the morning, waited on campus, and headed to Longjii Hotel where a dedicated section was set up for the competition.
* **Kickoff & Energy:** The event opened with guest and judge introductions. MC Nana Afia kept the energy high, followed by an insightful segment detailing what IEEE entails and its scope.
* **Final Sprint & Pitching:** Participating teams were given a final 30-minute window to finalize their builds before presenting to the judges.

![Winningteam-Aaenics26.jpeg](/images/upload_dd6a6d0962b23b92.jpeg)

---

## Key Observations & Winning Pitch
* A team consisting mostly of **Aaenics** members took first place with a brilliant, highly polished concept.
* **Judges' Feedback:** The evaluation session provided sharp, actionable feedback on value proposition, technical feasibility, and pitch delivery.

### Core Engineering Takeaway for Pitching:
> **Problem-First Framing:** When presenting an idea, the priority is to clearly illuminate the problem so the audience grasps its true weight. Follow it up with a practical, cost-effective solution your team can execute. Mastering this balance makes any pitch compelling.

---

*Note: Great event overall—and the food was definitely a bonus.*
![Winningteam-Aaenics26.jpeg](/images/upload_769e607d131225e8.jpeg)
